label: R², adjusted R² and model comparison — mastery test (unseen)

items.stem: With n = 50, k = 5 (parameters including the intercept) and R² = 0.55, the adjusted R² is:
items.explanation: R̄² = 1 − (1 − R²)(n − 1)/(n − k) = 1 − 0.45 × 49/45 = 1 − 0.49 = 0.51. The value 0.49 is the adjusted unexplained share, 0.45 is 1 − R², and 0.55 is R² itself.
items.check: Adjusted R² must lie below R² = 0.55, and with n large against k it must be only slightly below, which rules out 0.45 and 0.49.

items.stem: Adding an irrelevant regressor to a linear model with an intercept will:
options: decrease the residual sum of squares to zero
leave R² unchanged or increase it
items.explanation: Least squares can set the new coefficient to zero, so the residual sum of squares cannot rise and R² cannot fall. Adjusted R² can fall, and RSS reaches zero only when the model fits perfectly.

items.stem: The adjusted R² can be:
items.explanation: When R² is below (k − 1)/(n − 1) the adjustment pushes the value below zero. It cannot exceed 1, since the unexplained share is non-negative.

items.stem: A very high R² together with individually insignificant t statistics suggests:
options: a specification error in the dependent variable
items.explanation: Collinear regressors jointly explain y well, so R² and the overall F are high, while each coefficient has an inflated standard error and a small t. Autocorrelation and heteroscedasticity do not produce this pattern.

items.stem: In a linear model with an intercept, R² has which of these properties?
options: It always falls when a regressor is added
It is unaffected by the number of regressors
items.explanation: R² = 1 − RSS/TSS with 0 ≤ RSS ≤ TSS when the intercept is present. It never falls when a regressor is added, and it generally rises with the number of regressors.

items.stem: For the five points x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5, the fitted line has R² = 0.6. The adjusted R² (n = 5, k = 2) is:
items.explanation: R̄² = 1 − 0.4 × 4/3 = 1 − 0.5333 = 0.4667. Using n − k − 1 = 2 as the divisor gives 0.20, and inverting the ratio gives 0.70.
items.check: Adjusted R² must be below R² = 0.6 and, with n = 5, noticeably below; the value 0.60 is ruled out.

items.stem: Adding one regressor raises the adjusted R² exactly when the absolute value of its t statistic is:
items.explanation: R̄² = 1 − s²/s_y² rises exactly when s² falls, and s² falls exactly when t² > 1. Significance at 5% needs |t| near 2 and is a stricter requirement.

items.stem: With n = 20, k = 6 and R² = 0.10, the adjusted R² is:
items.explanation: R̄² = 1 − 0.9 × 19/14 = 1 − 1.2214 = −0.2214. The threshold (k − 1)/(n − 1) = 5/19 = 0.263 is above R² = 0.10, so the answer must be negative.
items.check: R² = 0.10 is below (k − 1)/(n − 1) = 0.263, so the adjusted value is negative; this rules out 0.10 and 0.22.

items.stem: Two nested models with n = 20 have RSS = 9000 (k = 2) and RSS = 5344 (k = 4). The F statistic for the two added coefficients is:
items.explanation: F = [(9000 − 5344)/2]/[5344/16] = 1828/334 = 5.47. Forgetting to divide by q = 2 gives 10.95, inverting the ratio gives 0.18, and 3.63 is the critical value rather than the statistic.
items.check: The numerator average, 1828, is about 5.5 times the denominator average, 334, so F lies between 5 and 6.

items.stem: Compared with AIC, the BIC penalty for each additional parameter is:
options: larger once n ≥ 8, since ln n exceeds 2
items.explanation: AIC adds 2 per parameter and BIC adds ln n, and ln 8 = 2.079 exceeds 2 while ln 7 = 1.946 does not. BIC therefore favours smaller models at all but tiny sample sizes.

items.stem: Regarding R² and adjusted R² in a linear model with an intercept.
items.explanation: R² never falls on adding a regressor, adjusted R² never exceeds R², and adjusted R² can be negative. Comparing R² across different dependent variables is invalid.
statements: R² never decreases when a regressor is added
R² can be used to compare a regression of y with a regression of ln y

A.why: The new coefficient can be set to zero.

C.why: The totals TSS differ because the dependent variables differ.

items.stem: A regression through the origin reports R² = 0.9227 while the same data with an intercept give 0.9868. The reported figure for the first model:
options: is the correlation between x and y
proves that the model without an intercept fits better
uses Σy² as the total, so it is not comparable with the second
items.explanation: Without an intercept the software measures RSS against Σy², not the total about the mean. The two figures use different denominators.

items.stem: In the comparison with n = 20, TSS = 72214, the larger model has k = 4 and RSS = 5344 (R² = 0.926). Its adjusted R² is:
items.explanation: R̄² = 1 − (5344/16)/(72214/19) = 1 − 334/3800.7 = 0.9121. The value 0.93 is the R² rounded and 0.87 is the smaller model's adjusted R².
items.check: Adjusted R² must be below R² = 0.926, which rules out 0.93.

items.stem: For a subset regression with little omitted-variable bias, Mallows' Cp is expected to be:
options: close to the number of parameters p
items.explanation: Cp estimates the standardised total error of the subset model. Without bias its expected value is about p. A Cp far above p signals omitted variables.

items.stem: Two models for the same dependent variable have AIC values of 119.76 and 126.19. The preferred model is:
options: neither, because AIC needs nested models
the one with the larger R² in all cases
items.explanation: A smaller AIC is better, and AIC can compare non-nested models for the same y. The larger-R² model need not have the smaller AIC, because AIC charges for parameters.

items.stem: On comparing regression models.
items.explanation: The nested F needs nested models, AIC and BIC apply to non-nested models for the same y, and BIC's heavier penalty tends to pick smaller models. R² cannot pick the smallest model, since it never falls with more regressors.
statements: The nested F test requires one model to be a restricted version of the other
AIC and BIC can compare non-nested models with the same dependent variable
Maximising R² picks the smallest adequate model
BIC's larger penalty tends to favour smaller models than AIC does

A.why: The test is built on the drop in RSS from restrictions.

B.why: They need only the likelihood and the number of parameters.

C.why: R² never falls with extra regressors, so maximising it picks the largest model.

items.stem: With the 20-observation data, the restricted model (k = 2, RSS = 9000) has Mallows' Cp, using σ̂² = 5344/16 = 334 from the full model, equal to:
items.explanation: Cp = RSS_p/σ̂² − (n − 2p) = 9000/334 − (20 − 4) = 26.95 − 16 = 10.95. The value 26.95 omits the correction, and p = 2 is the target for an unbiased model.
items.check: A Cp near p = 2 would indicate no bias. The value 10.95 is far above it, agreeing with the significant F.

items.stem: A simple regression with n = 1000 has R² = 0.01. The adjusted R² to four decimals is:
items.explanation: R̄² = 1 − 0.99 × 999/998 = 1 − 0.99100 = 0.0090. With n this large the adjustment is small, but it does reduce the figure slightly.
items.check: Adjusted R² must be a little below R² = 0.01, so it cannot equal 0.0100 and cannot be negative.

items.stem: The AIC of the restricted model is 126.19 and of the full model 119.76, with the same dependent variable. The AIC difference is:
items.explanation: 126.19 − 119.76 = 6.43. Doubling gives 12.85 and halving gives 3.22. A difference above about 6 is usually read as strong support for the lower-AIC model.
items.check: The difference must equal the gap between the two AIC values given, a little over 6.

items.stem: For y = 10, 12, 13, 15, 16 on x = 1..5, the line through the origin has slope 3.8727. Measured against the total about the mean, its R² is:
items.explanation: RSS about the origin line is far larger than TSS about the mean, so 1 − RSS/TSS is −2.031. The reported 0.9227 uses Σy² as the total, and 0.99 is the R² of the model with an intercept.
items.check: A line forced through the origin through data far from the origin fits worse than a horizontal line at the mean, so the centred R² must be negative.
